o: JUVENTUTI AMERICANAE Jo. Bened. Diaz Gamarra S. vigiliasque. Vestra omnium res agitur, Juvenes ingenio praestantissimi, & praeter ceteras gentes ad Scientias comparati. Vestra nunc res agitur. Neque enim doctis ego Viris, qui se Philosophiam, qualem illam cunque biennii labore (nec admodùm improbo) adsequutos esse arbitrantur; neque verò iis haec conscripta volui, & nuncupata, qui totos dies ê suggestu Scholari tanquam ex trípode, de rebus multò difficillimis, non item multò sibi compertissimis (*), pronunciant. Sed vobis, Juvenes, qui sacra haec primùm adoriemini, humanae Philosophiae, quî nihil jucundius esse potest, arcem, ubi aliquando tandem liceat, ingressuri. Vobis, magna Patriae spes, Recentioris Philosophiae Institutiones, brevissimè quidem hinc inde excerptas subjicio, longè alia daturus, benè multa, nisi adeò breve curriculum Scholae esset, quod de more vobis est percurrendum. Age verò, & quoniam
e: Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra sends greetings and his lucubrations. Your cause, all of you, is at stake, young men of most excellent talent, fitted beyond other nations for the Sciences. It is your cause that is now at stake. For I did not wish these pages to be written for, or dedicated to, learned Men who think they have attained Philosophy, such as it is, by the labor of two years (and not very strenuous labor at that); nor to those who all day long pronounce from the School’s lectern, as from a tripod, on matters exceedingly difficult and not equally well known to themselves (*). But to you, young men, who are now for the first time approaching these sacred rites, and who are about to enter, when at length it may be allowed, the citadel of human Philosophy, than which nothing can be more delightful. To you, great hope of our Country, I submit these Institutions of the Newer Philosophy, excerpted, very briefly indeed, from here and there; and I would give you far other things, and a good many of them, were the course of the Schools not so short, which by custom you must run through. But come, and since it was for your sake

o: (*) Cl. Melch. Cano Lib. VIII. de Loc. Theolog. [PDF 2] vestri gratiâ hoc muneris ac laboris susceptum est, quid scribendo praestiterim, aut saltem conatus fuerim, paucis accipite. Principio enim, Philosophiae quam adgredimini, Historiam, breviusculè exaratam in ipso Institutionum limine, etiam atque etiam vobis commendo. Ipsam perlegite, volvite, meditamini, ac reputate cum animis vestris, quanti momenti futura sit ad Philosophiam ipsam rectè atque ordine perdiscendam. Nam ubi nescias, quid Philosophia sit, sub quibus Auctoribus nata, quousque apud majores nostros, & quo tandem in pretio habita, quae fata, qui progressus, quae via ratioque docendi; omninò fieri non potest quin passim turpiter erres. Cujus erroris genus non aliud magis, meâ quidem sententiâ, cavendum vitandumque est? quàm eorum, quibus hoc unum ad veram philosophiam refertur, quod pueri imberbesque ipsi didicerint; cetera pro nihilo ducunt, quasi vana fingentis aegri somnia essent. Quocirca meritò ridentur.
e: (*) The renowned Melchor Cano, bk. VIII of De locis theologicis. [PDF 2] sake that this task and labor were undertaken, hear in a few words what I have accomplished in writing, or at least have attempted. First of all, then, I commend to you again and again the History of the Philosophy you are entering upon, set down rather briefly at the very threshold of the Institutions. Read it through, turn it over, meditate on it, and weigh in your minds how important it will be for learning Philosophy itself thoroughly, correctly and in due order. For if you do not know what Philosophy is, under what Authors it was born, how far and in what esteem it was held among our forebears, what its fortunes were, what its progress, what its way and method of teaching, it cannot possibly be that you will not err shamefully at every turn. And no kind of error, in my opinion at least, is more to be guarded against and avoided than that of those for whom this alone counts as true philosophy, what they themselves learned as beardless boys; everything else they hold as nothing, as though it were the empty dreams of a sick man’s fancy. For which reason they are deservedly laughed at. Others, however, and indeed very many in these times, are so delighted both by Aristotle and, above all, by what, under the name of so great

o: Alios autem, & quidem plurimos hac tempestate, cùm Aristoteles, tùm vero quae [PDF 3] tanti Viri nomine (nam ultro fatemur, summum utique virum fuisse) vulgò in Scholis venditantur, adeò delectant, ut seriò adfirment, non aliud aptius commodiusve ad exacuenda puerorum ingeniola, & ad Sacram Theologiam dissertè atque eruditè tradendam inveniri unquam posse, quàm exercitamenta illa sempiterna, concertationes, logomachias De Universalibus, De Ente rationis, De Formis substantialibus, De Unione, & toto Composito, & sexcentis id genus aliis, quibus ingenia torquentur quidem, adteruntur; at timeo nè nihilo acutiora fiant ad sapientiae studium, & optimas disciplinas, quò nostra omnis vis ac cogitatio, tanquam ad scopum, collimare debet. ¿Ecquid autem, amabo, vanissima illa Mahumedanorum Avicennae, Averrois, Alpharabii, & reliquae Arabum turbae interpretamenta, ad veram religionem, ad Christi Ecclesiam, ad Sacram denique Theologiam emolumenti adferre poterunt? Scilicet venerandi Ecclesiae Patres, majores nostri, nunc apud Caelites Conscripti, Dionysius Areopagita, Ephremus, Irenaeus, Cyprianus, Athanasius, Epiphanius, uterque Gregorius,
e: ¶¶¶ [PDF 3] a Man (for we freely admit that he was certainly a very great man), is commonly peddled in the Schools, that they seriously affirm that nothing fitter or more convenient could ever be found for sharpening the little wits of boys, and for teaching Sacred Theology eloquently and learnedly, than those everlasting exercises, the disputes and logomachies On Universals, On the Being of Reason, On Substantial Forms, On the Union and the Whole Composite, and six hundred others of that kind, by which minds are indeed tortured and worn down; but I fear they grow no sharper for the pursuit of wisdom and for the best disciplines, at which all our strength and thought ought to aim, as at a target. And what profit, pray, will those utterly empty interpretations of the Mahometans Avicenna, Averroes, Alfarabi, and the rest of the Arab throng be able to bring to the true religion, to the Church of Christ, and finally to Sacred Theology? No doubt the venerable Fathers of the Church, our forebears, now Fathers Conscript among the dwellers in heaven, Dionysius the Areopagite, Ephrem, Irenaeus, Cyprian, Athanasius, Epiphanius, both Gregories, Chrysostom,

Basil, Leo, Hilary, Prosper, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, did not themselves also either defend the Church, or discourse on Theological matters, or rout the profane innovators, the Heretics. On the contrary, they did so above all: for their golden volumes bear witness to it. And yet one would look for Aristotle there in vain. Not that these very great men were ignorant of dialectic and syllogisms, or ordered them banished altogether when matters of the very gravest weight were to be treated or debated: a thing which, had it been done, would have been done quite rashly and heedlessly (yet it was not done by them), and which we would by no means imitate, since the subtleties of syllogisms do not so greatly displease us. But, as I judge, admonished by the saying of Paul, where he says: Beware lest any man cheat you by philosophy, and vain deceit, these most Holy Men resolved, in holiness, to treat all those things which pertain, by God’s revelation, to holiness of life and to everlasting beatitude: from which, assuredly, the whole Philosophy of the Heathen is all but alien. Let them cease, therefore, to deafen our ears, and even to tear us and ours to pieces with abuse, who think they cannot approach Sacred Theology

o: Chrysostomus, Basilius, Leo, Hilarius, Prosper, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, non ipsi quoque aut Ecclesiam tutati sunt, aut de rebus Theologicis disseruere, aut prophanos novatores Haereticos profligârunt. Imo verò maximè: id enim aurea volumina testantur. Atqui frustra quisquam ibi Aristotelem requirat. Non quòd summi viri dialecticen & syllogismos ignorârint, aut penitus exulare jusserint, dum esset de rebus multò gravissimis agendum, disceptandumvè: id quod omninò temerè atque oscitanter factum (nec tamen ab iis factum) nos haudquaquam imitaremur, quippè quibus syllogismorum acumina non adeò displicent. Sed, ut ego arbitror, Pauli effato commonefacti, dum ait: Videte, ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam, & inanem fallaciam, Sanctissimi Viri sanctè sibi tractanda omnia voluerunt, quae ad vitae sanctimoniam, & sempiternam beatitudinem, Deo revelante, pertinerent: à quibus profectò parum abest, quin tota Ethnicorum Philosophia abhorreat. Desinant ergo nobis aures obtundere, maledictis etiam nos nostraque lacerare, qui se non antè Sacram Theologiam [PDF 5] adgredi posse putant, quàm integras quaestiuncularum centurias in discrimen vocaverint. Nisi fortean ii (quod vehementer equidem suspicor, doleoque) non Sacram denique Theologiam, quae divina prorsus scientia est; sed Theologiae fumum atque umbram consectantur, nubem pro Junone amplexati, quod est in proverbio. At enimvero, inquies, Divum Albertum cognomento Magnum, Divum THOMAM AQUINATEM, (ut nihil interim de Div. Johanne Damasceno) Divum quoque Bonamventuram, ceterosque recentioris aevi Theologos, Sapientissimos Viros, consilio, maturitate, moribus spectabiles, Petrum Lombardum, Scotum, Halesium, multos in disceptando fuisse, non operosas quaestiones, non syllogismos, non Aristotelem dedignatos: cui Philosopho auctoritatem plurimam quòd saepè tribuerint, non ideò tamen quasi inferioris subsellii Philosophos, ac minimè dissertos Theologos, tantos Viros jure quisquam reprehendat. ¿Nonnè compertissima haec sunt, & posita ante omnium oculos, meridie ipso clariora? Ajo. Sed quoniam ejus rei men-
e: ¶¶¶2 [PDF 5] until they have called whole hundreds of petty questions into contest. Unless perhaps these men (as I strongly suspect, and grieve) are pursuing not, after all, Sacred Theology, which is an altogether divine science, but the smoke and shadow of Theology, having embraced a cloud for Juno, as the proverb has it. But surely, you will say, St. Albert, surnamed the Great, St. Thomas Aquinas (to say nothing for the moment of St. John Damascene), St. Bonaventure too, and the other Theologians of the more recent age, Most Wise Men, admirable for counsel, maturity and character, Peter Lombard, Scotus, Alexander of Hales, were much given to disputation, and did not disdain laborious questions, nor syllogisms, nor Aristotle: and because they often attributed very great authority to this Philosopher, no one could rightly reproach such great Men on that account, as though they were Philosophers of a lower bench and Theologians of little eloquence. Are not these things most certain, and set before the eyes of all, clearer than noonday itself? I grant it. But since mention of this matter

o: [PDF 6] tio incidit, circunspecto autem maturèque dicto opus est: rem, si placet, ordine persequamur. Ad Divum THOMAM quod adtinet, (nam de ceteris omnibus posteà dicendum) nemo unquam mortalium plura, nemo solertiùs, eruditiùs, temperatiùs, nemo breviùs omnia complexus est, quae ad Sacram Theologiam spectare, aut quoquo pacto referri posse viderentur. ¡Deus immortalis! quale Viro ingenium! quanta disceptandi copia! quàm adsidua, quàm multa in evolvendis Sacrae Paginae voluminibus diligentia! quàm fuit ille veritus Sanctos Ecclesiae Patres! quàm incredibile ac penè divinum ejus, cernendo difficillima, acumen illud mentis prorsùs Angelicae! quis in scribendo candor, quae docendo méthodus, severitas in judicando! Verè utique dixeris (id quod in re satis absimili Cicero prior dixerat) Divi THOMAE AQUINATIS libros, ac praesertim SUMMAM illam THEOLOGICAM, omnium Theologorum bibliothecas, fremant omnes licet, & maximarum rerum ubertate, & auctoritatis robore longè multumque superare. Plura enim Div.
e: [PDF 6] has come up, and it calls for circumspect and well-considered speech, let us, if you please, pursue the matter in order. As for St. Thomas (for of all the others I must speak afterwards), no mortal ever embraced more, none more skillfully, more learnedly, more temperately, none more briefly, all the things that seemed to bear upon Sacred Theology, or could in any way be referred to it. Immortal God! what genius the Man had! what abundance in disputation! how constant, how great his diligence in unrolling the volumes of the Sacred Page! how he revered the Holy Fathers of the Church! how incredible and almost divine that acumen of his altogether Angelic mind in discerning the most difficult things! what candor in writing, what method in teaching, what severity in judging! You might truly say (as Cicero had said before, in a matter not very unlike) that the books of St. Thomas Aquinas, and especially that Theological Summa, though all should roar against it, far and greatly surpass the libraries of all the Theologians, both in the abundance of the greatest matters and in the strength of authority. For St. Thomas

o: [PDF 7] THOMAS immortali suâ & plusquàm Sallustianâ brevitate in rem Theologicam invexit, adprimè erudita, ac scitu dignissima, quàm plerique ceteri concupiverunt. Haec autem Divum THOMAM Theologum egregia laus manet, manebitque quandiù scientiae honos erit. Quòd si interdum (nam eò, unde discesseram, redeo) Aristoteli auctoritatem tribuere disceptando solet, invitus quidem fecit, ubi de Sacra Doctrina ageretur. Nisi velis, summum Virum adeò hebetem ingenio, adeò etiam ineptum atque oscitantem fuisse, ut quae consultò in superioribus, Art. nimirum VIII. Quaest. I. statuerat, de minuenda omnium auctoritate praeterquam divinae revelationis, Apostolis & Prophetis factae, qui Canonicos Libros scripserunt; eadem posteà exemplo suo ipsemet, datâ operâ infirmaret. Sin verò de Divo THOMA, non Theologo, sed planè Philosopho, quaeritur, mementote, non jam THOMAM illum AQUINATEM Ecclesiae lumen atque ornamentum; sed Ethnicum (ex impio pium recens factum) Philosophum, nomine Aristotelem, negotium vobis facéssere, quod propemodùm
e: [PDF 7] brought into Theology, with his immortal and more than Sallustian brevity, more things, exceedingly learned and most worth knowing, than most others even desired. And this outstanding praise of St. Thomas as a Theologian remains, and will remain as long as learning is held in honor. But if at times (for I return to the point from which I had digressed) he is wont in disputing to attribute authority to Aristotle, he did so unwillingly indeed, where Sacred Doctrine was in question. Unless you would have it that so great a Man was so dull of wit, so inept too and heedless, that what he had deliberately laid down in the preceding pages, namely in Art. VIII of Quest. I, about diminishing the authority of all save that of divine revelation, made to the Apostles and Prophets who wrote the Canonical Books, he himself afterwards weakened on purpose by his own example. But if the question concerns St. Thomas not as Theologian but plainly as Philosopher, remember that it is not now that Thomas Aquinas, the light and ornament of the Church, but a Heathen Philosopher (lately made pious from impious), Aristotle by name, who is making trouble for you, a trouble which will amount to next to nothing.

o: nullum erit. ¿Nam quotusquisque nescit, Angelicum Doctorem repurgâsse quidem Peripateticam Philosophiam, sexcentis passim erroribus commaculatam, ceterùm quod reliquum erat, non idcircò firmum, ratum, sanctum denique fore voluisse, nisi quod invicta ratio suadéret? ¿Ubinam ergo sunt, qui nos de oppugnato laesove Divo THOMA toties postulârunt? praepósteri homines, quibus satiùs multò fuisset strenuam operam in legendo Divum THOMAM navâsse, quod minimè isti faciunt; quàm sedentibus otiosisque, per summam ignaviam, quae nè adtigére quidem, aut certe non adsequuntur, ludibrio, joco esse. Sed haec hactenus. Venio nunc ad reliqua: nimirùm Divi Jo. Damascenus, Antoninus, Albertus, Bonaventura: Doctores post hominum memoriam praeclarissimi, Scotus, Halesius, (nam Episcopo Parisiensi alia mens fuerat) neque quaestiones, hoc est, ancipites illas controversias multùm in Scholis agitari sólitas, neque syllogismos, neque Aristotelem aspernantur. ¿An verò nos aspernamur, aut disceptationibus Scholae bellum indicimus? Pro-
e: For how few do not know that the Angelic Doctor did indeed purge the Peripatetic Philosophy, stained everywhere with six hundred errors, but that he did not on that account wish what remained to be firm, ratified, and in a word sacrosanct, except what unconquered reason urged? Where, then, are those who have so often arraigned us for attacking or injuring St. Thomas? Perverse men, for whom it would have been far better to have spent strenuous effort in reading St. Thomas, which is the last thing they do, than, sitting idle, out of utter sloth, to make a mockery and a jest of things they do not even touch, or at least do not grasp. But enough of this. I come now to the rest: namely Sts. John Damascene, Antoninus, Albert, Bonaventure, Doctors most illustrious within the memory of man, Scotus, Hales (for the Bishop of Paris had been of another mind), do not spurn questions, that is, those doubtful controversies much agitated in the Schools, nor syllogisms, nor Aristotle. And do we, then, spurn them, or declare war on the disputations of the School? Assuredly

o: [PDF 9] fectò res ipsa loquitur: & nos quoque seculo nostro, Magistrisque, quorum magna apud nostrates existimatio est, morem gessimus, quaestiones, syllogismos, postremò Aristotelem ipsum, ubi rectè sápere visus erat, complexi; omnia tamen, pro viribus atque inertia nostra, sobriè, prudenter, temperatè. Nam vel ipsum brevitatis studium, quod omninò curae cordique esse debuit, nos, tametsi aliter, aut multò plura scribendi operae pretium foret, perstringere tamen calamum coëgisset, nè Juvenes tyrones nostros obrueremus. Et quoniam satis multa hucusque praemisimus, tanquam vindicias nostras, ne quis (ut ferè fit) silentium in conscientiam duceret: superest, ut nonnihil de instituto operis nostri breviter subjungamus. Et primùm quidem philosophiam, non vulgarem, stylo paullulùm limatiori quàm vulgò traditur, exaratam, vobis exhibemus, eamque cùm arctissimè quàm fieri potuit, tùm etiam apertissimè, atque omnibus numeris absolutam: ut prodigio simile quiddam factum mihi, persuasum haberem, nisi pleraque omnia ex
e: [PDF 9] the thing speaks for itself: we too have humored our age, and our Masters, who are held in great esteem among our countrymen, embracing questions, syllogisms, and finally Aristotle himself, where he seemed to judge rightly; but all of it, as far as our strength and our want of skill allowed, soberly, prudently, temperately. For the very pursuit of brevity, which ought to have been our whole care and concern, would have compelled us to restrain the pen, even had it otherwise been worth the trouble to write much more, lest we overwhelm our young recruits. And since we have set forth enough so far, by way of our defense, lest anyone (as usually happens) should take our silence for a bad conscience, it remains for us to add briefly something about the plan of our work. And first, we present to you a philosophy that is not the common one, set down in a style a little more polished than that in which it is commonly taught, and that both as concisely as could be done and also as plainly as possible, and complete in every respect: so that I would be persuaded that I had done something like a marvel, had not nearly everything come from all the best

o: optimis quibusque recentioris aevi Philosophis, magno labore, summâ item fide decerpsissem. Quod unum mihi jure tribuo, ratus, non mediocri vel ad id ipsum diligentiâ opus esse: proindè aliquammultam vos olim, Juvenes, gratiam, sin minus vivo, at saltim extincto relaturos. ¿Quid enim? Plus centum volumina, nec oscitanter tamen, evolvi, priusquam ad haec Elementa conscribenda manum admovérem. Oculis omnia circunspexi, diu noctuque chartis impallescere in animum induxi, quò Juventuti nostrae consúlerem. ¿Quid plura? Otium ego meum, [si quid reliqui D. O. M. facit adsiduè pro Christo JESU laborantibus] dulcis Patriae domicilium; aes, grande satis, quod impensum mihi est; &, quod mortales pluris habere solent, famam, nominisque existimationem (quippè qui eversae Philosophiae, & avítae maiorum religionis reus apud imperitum vulgus agor); cuncta haec tanti profectò feci, ut maioris quidem, aut certè multò maximi, vestram institutionem ac disciplinam mihi faciendam putarem.
e: Philosophers of the newer age, culled with great labor and likewise with the utmost fidelity. This alone I rightly claim for myself, judging that no ordinary diligence was needed even for that very task: and therefore that you, young men, will one day render me no small thanks, if not while I live, then at least when I am dead. For what? I turned over more than a hundred volumes, and not carelessly either, before I set my hand to writing these Elements. I surveyed everything with my own eyes; I resolved to grow pale over papers day and night, so as to provide for our Youth. What more? My leisure [if God, Best and Greatest, leaves any to those who labor without rest for Christ Jesus], my home in my sweet Country; money, a sum large enough, which I have spent; and, what mortals are wont to hold dearer, my reputation and the good opinion of my name (since I am arraigned before the ignorant crowd as guilty of overthrowing Philosophy and the ancestral religion of our forefathers): all these I have valued, to be sure, but only so far as to judge that your instruction and training were to be held of greater worth, or rather by far the greatest. But in truth, it is a newer philosophy that I myself

o: Verum enimverò recentiorem ipse phi- [PDF 11] losophiam adfero. ¿Quidni adferrem? At tota haeretica est, inquiunt, & ex imis Erebi Orcique sedibus dudùm excitata, nimirum qualem apud exteras gentes Ambubajárum collegia, pharmacopólae, Mendíci, mimae, balatrónes, hoc genus omne, dum ingenio suo nimiùm indulgent, dum Christi Ecclesiam funditùs evertere moliuntur, quasi aliud quiddam agentes, cum Schola Peripatetica fidem ipsi ii orthodoxam, Christianam religionem, sanctissimos tot jam secula mores, corrumpunt, pessumdant, perditum eunt. ¿Itanè verò? O praeclaros, vigilantes, egregios Ecclesiae custodes! Scilicet, quem vos pro deo philosophiae colitis, Aristóteles, is denique orthodoxus erat, is pietate ac religione insignis. ¿Sed quid adtinet nunc de his plura? Suam quisque ferè tuetur philosophiam, à maioribus acceptam, tanquam deos aliquos penates, quos oppugnari, vinci, diripi, acerbissimè doleat. Vos igitur, Juvenes, moneo obtestorque, ne quis vestrûm ab incoepto harum Institutionum & recentioris Philosophiae cur-
e: ¶¶*¶ [PDF 11] bring forward. And why should I not bring it forward? But it is wholly heretical, they say, and was long ago raised up from the lowest seats of Erebus and Orcus, such, namely, as is found among foreign nations, where The guilds of flute-girls, the quack-druggists, Beggars, actresses, buffoons, all that breed, while they indulge their own wit too freely, while they strive to overturn the Church of Christ from its foundations, as though about some other business, these very men, together with the Peripatetic School, corrupt, ruin and go about to destroy the orthodox faith, the Christian religion, and the morals held most holy for so many centuries now. Is it so indeed? O splendid, watchful, excellent guardians of the Church! Of course Aristotle, whom you worship as the god of philosophy, was orthodox after all, he was outstanding in piety and religion. But what is the point of saying more about these things now? Each man, as a rule, defends his own philosophy, received from his forebears, as if it were some household gods, and would grieve most bitterly to see them attacked, conquered, plundered. I warn and adjure you, therefore, young men, that none of you, from the course once begun of these Institutions and of the newer Philosophy,

o: [PDF 12] riculo pedem referre velit, neu patiatur sibi fucum ab imperitis fieri, qui rectam docendi discendique viam cane peius & angue perhorrescunt, fugiunt, aversantur, nè latum unguem à prisca Scholae consuetudine discedere ausi: quasi religio iis esset cum antiquioribus praejudicatò errare malle quàm cum aliis vera sentire [*], aut denique verosimillimis
e: [PDF 12] be willing to draw back his foot, nor let himself be imposed upon by the ignorant, who dread the right way of teaching and learning worse than a dog or a snake, shun it, turn away from it, not daring to depart a nail’s breadth from the ancient custom of the School: as though it were a point of religion with them to prefer erring, by prejudgment, with the ancients to thinking the truth with others [*], or, in short, to acquiesce in the most probable ¶¶*¶2                           where

o: (*) Praeclariss. Doctor nostras trienniò antè in lucem edidit Librum, cui titulum fecerat LA LOGICA DE D. ANDRES PIQUER, ubi adeò multus est in re rehendendo (acerbè satis, ne dicam jejunè atque ineptè) quoscunque unquàm legerit Recentiores, ut propè fúrere ipsum dixeris, non ratiocinari. Verulamium, Arnaldum, Cartesium, Gassendum, Mallebranchium, Lockium, Heineccium, Wolffium, Genuensem, Verneyum, sus deque habet, quasi rem Logicam ipsi non auxerint, sed perfunctoriè modo tractaverint. Unus Aristoteles magnus & clarus existimatur, post quem unus PIQUERUS Logices praecepta tradidit; ceteri meras nugas, & quae ad rem minimè pertinebant, saepius inculcavere. Tanta profectò erat Clariss. viri PHILAUTIA, (ipse autem more suo dicat, quae sit Latinè, Graecè, Hispanè, ejus vocabuli potestas) & praeconcepta vetustatis opinio, ut venerandum illum Senem, aevi nunc senescentis atque Hispaniae nostrae ornamentum, fato suo recens functum excitârit, P. BENED. HIERONYMUM FEIJOÓ, quem eo nomine traducit, quòd Recentiores ex antè nominatis quosdam sine discrimine laudâsset. [PDF 13] adquiescere, ubi veriora praestò non erunt. Cujus farinae obtrectatores, quaerulos, difficiles, leviores etiam quàm sibi fingere quisquam posset subacti ingenii viros, quos neque in arundine equitare, neque nuces, & par impar delectet: hos, inquam, ne auditóte. Putidi enim vanique sunt. Quòd si postremo id loco nobis objecerint, frustrà in lucem haec decerpta nostra edi in gratiam Juventutis, quum aliae Institutiones non desint, antehac typis evulgatae: ostendant ij, quaeso, ubinam tandem reperire sit (quod diu multumque quaesivimus) doctrinam recentiorem, more ab Scholis omninò non abhorrente, & cùm brevissimè traditam tùm planam illam satis, apertam, ordine congestam, adornatam, atque (id quod maximum est) utilem futuram in reliqua vita (*). (*) Agitur enim hîc de DEI EXISTENTIA, DE ANIMORUM IMMORTALITATE: refelluntur religionis hostes infensissimi MATERIALISTAE, DEISTAE, FATALISTAE &c: traduntur GEOMETRICA, ETHICA, PSYCHOLOGICA: postremò nihil deesse videtur, quod jure quisquam requirat, ex iis, quae ad JUVENUM institutionem pertinebunt.
e: (*) A most distinguished Doctor, a countryman of ours, three years ago brought to light a Book to which he had given the title La Lógica de D. Andrés Piquer, in which he is so prolix in censuring (harshly enough, not to say jejunely and ineptly) whatever Moderns he has ever read, that you would almost say he raves rather than reasons. Bacon, Arnauld, Descartes, Gassendi, Malebranche, Locke, Heineccius, Wolff, Genovesi, Verney he holds of no account, as if they had not advanced Logic themselves but only treated it perfunctorily. Aristotle alone is esteemed great and famous, after whom Piquer alone handed down the precepts of Logic; the rest have all too often inculcated mere trifles, and things not at all to the point. So great indeed was the most distinguished man’s philautia (let him tell us himself, in his usual way, what the force of that word is in Latin, Greek and Spanish), and his preconceived opinion in favor of antiquity, that he has roused that venerable Old Man, the ornament of our now aging century and of our Spain, lately gone to his fate, Fr. Benito Jerónimo Feijóo, whom he holds up to ridicule on the ground that he had praised some of the Moderns named above without discrimination. [PDF 13] where truer things will not be at hand. Detractors of this stamp, querulous, difficult, more frivolous even than anyone could imagine men of mature mind to be, whom riding on a reed, and nuts, and odd-and-even no longer delight: these, I say, do not listen to. For they are tiresome and empty. But if, finally, they object to us that it is useless for these extracts of ours to be published for the benefit of Youth, since other Institutions, already made public in print, are not lacking: let them show, I beg, where at length one may find (what we have long and much sought) a newer doctrine, in a manner not at all at odds with the Schools, and both very briefly delivered and also sufficiently plain, open, arranged in order, adorned, and (what matters most) likely to be useful in the rest of life (*). It (*) For here the subjects treated are the Existence of God and the Immortality of Souls; the most bitter enemies of religion, the Materialists, Deists, Fatalists, etc., are refuted; Geometry, Ethics, Psychology are taught: in short, nothing seems to be lacking that anyone could rightly require, of the things that will pertain to the instruction of Youth.

o: Dolendum verò mihi est, hasce meas Institutiones, minutioribus, neque tamen paribus & concinnis typis editum iri: quod ob typographicae rei inopiam in hoc terrarum orbe, & temporis angustias, invito ac reluctanti contigerit. Vos autem facilè ignoscetis, non culpae quidem, sed quòd deforme quiddam atque absurdum volumina praeseferant; accuratiora, emendatiora, pulchriora in dies, si Superis placet, expectantes, quae polliceor equidem vobis. Pergite verò, Juvenes, ut coepistis, & ampliss. Domino Praesuli nostro Michchuacanensi D. LUDOVICO FERDINANDO DE HOYOS ET MIER grates quàm potestis maximas unà mecum rependite: quòd munificentissimâ erga nos benivolentiâ singulari studiorum rationem in hoc Perillustri Colleg. Salesiano etiam atque etiam diligenter habendam, in animum suspiciendus Vir suum, celsum quidem, & ad optima quaevis paratissimum, induxerit: quòd recentioris philosophiae Institutiones, vobis jam pridem â me traditas é suggestu Academico nostro, non probârit modò, verum etiam laudando concelebraverit: quodque huma-
e: It grieves me, though, that these Institutions of mine are to be printed in type that is smaller, and yet neither uniform nor elegant: a thing that has befallen me against my will and to my reluctance, owing to the poverty of the printing trade in this part of the world and to the shortness of time. But you will readily forgive, not a fault indeed, but the fact that the volumes display something unsightly and awkward, looking forward to more accurate, more correct, more handsome ones from day to day, if it please the Powers above, which I for my part promise you. Go on, then, young men, as you have begun, and together with me render the greatest thanks you can to our most illustrious Lord Prelate of Michoacán, Don Luis Fernando de Hoyos y Mier: because, with most munificent benevolence toward us, he, a Man to be looked up to, brought his mind, lofty indeed and most ready for every good thing, to take singular and ever more diligent care of the order of studies in this Most Illustrious College of St. Francis de Sales; because he not only approved the Institutions of the newer philosophy, long since delivered to you by me from our Academic chair, but even celebrated them with praise; and because, most kindly

o: [PDF 15] nissimè exceptos me vosque clientes, ac dulciori vocabulo filios, paternâ caritate, & semper summopere expetendâ benedictione prosequatur. Faxit Deus O. M. ut Ecclesiae nostrae bono atque ornamento quàm diutissimè praesit. Dabam Mexici, ubi edendis per typos Institutionibus totus incumbebam, a. d. Calend. Septembres, anno Domini CIƆ IƆ CC LXXIV. N. B. Orthographicam rationem eam ferè secuti sumus, quàm viri Eruditissimi Heineccius, Verneyusque cùm praeceptionibus saepè tùm saepius exemplis magis probavêre. Quod ideò animadversum volumus, nè quis arbitretur, novandi studio id praestitum à nobis fuisse. Typographicos aerores (si qui supersunt) posteriores curae, quum recudendi operis copia erit, emendabunt.

We have for the most part followed that system of spelling which the most Learned men Heineccius and Verney commended, often by precepts and more often still by examples. We wished this to be noted so that no one may think it was done by us out of a love of novelty.
